sources.description:
I am an LLM researcher working on optimization and efficient training of neural networks. My current research includes low-rank pretraining, spectral regularization, parameter-efficient fine-tuning, and reducing the memory cost of language-model training.

I study how optimization and regularization affect the singular-value spectra and effective rank of weight matrices. I am interested in spectral weight decay, nuclear-norm regularization, proximal methods, and Newton-Schulz approximations. A central question is whether training can make a model easier to compress with low-rank factorization while preserving its quality. Related questions concern generalization and memorization under label noise.

Another research direction is optimization for LoRA and other low-rank parameterizations. Relevant topics include Muon-style matrix updates, optimization of factorized weights, rebalancing, spectral constraints, and convergence analysis. I want to understand both the geometry of these updates and their practical behavior when fine-tuning language models.

I also work on memory-efficient LLM pretraining. Relevant methods include low-rank gradient and optimizer-state representations, GaLore, Frugal-style methods, and low-precision optimizer states such as FP8. I am interested in their tradeoffs between model quality, training memory, throughput, and communication cost, including how those tradeoffs change with model scale.

As a secondary current interest, I am building an AI research digest agent with a handwritten harness. Relevant work includes explicit context management, structured LLM decisions, application-controlled tools, and paper retrieval and relevance ranking using lexical or embedding-based methods.

I have not specified hard topic exclusions for this digest.

passages.text: Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) often underperforms full fine-tuning, especially in heterogeneous and continual-learning settings in which substantial forgetting occurs. In general, it suffers from an undesirable learning–forgetting trade-off across diverse fine-tuning settings. We identify a potential contributor: LoRA adapters, especially high-rank ones, frequently fail to realize the available capacity afforded by the configured rank. Specifically, we find that standard LoRA updates have effective rank far below their configured rank, limiting how broadly the update energy is distributed. Therefore, we propose training mechanisms that optimize the original objective while maximizing adapter effective rank. Our main method adds a simple, stable, differentiable, and SVD-free Rényi-2 effective-rank regularizer to the language-modeling loss. We also connect capacity maximization to norm-bounded updates. In mixed-domain rank sweeps on three models evaluated with multiple random seeds, a penalty weight of λ = 0.01 \lambda=0.01 lowers mean Wiki perplexity at every tested rank of at least 16 16 relative to unpenalized LoRA. Mean training perplexity improves or increases by at most 0.02 0.02 in all but one model–rank comparison. Single-task and scheduling experiments further show that the balance between learning and retention depends on the configuration. We also observe that several LoRA variants in the literature also suffer from the identified capacity issue, and our approach provides a complementary axis of improvement to LoRA-based parameter-efficient fine-tuning. These results suggest that effective rank is not only a post-hoc diagnostic of adapter quality, but a trainable objective for improving the learning–forgetting frontier. Our code is available at

Language-model post-training changes a model’s behavior by changing its weights. Supervised fine-tuning ( sft ) learns from demonstration responses, while reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards ( rlvr ) learns from sampled responses scored by an automatic checker. Weight-space measurements describe how these procedures alter a pretrained model and inform methods that operate on weight differences, including task arithmetic and low-rank adaptation ( Ilharco et al., 2023 ; Hu et al., 2022 ) . Interpreting those measurements requires separating the mathematical object being measured from the functional applied to it. That distinction matters when comparing recent accounts of post-training geometry. Mukherjee et al. (2025) report sparse, nearly full-algebraic-rank rlvr updates. Zhu et al. (2025) analyze update localization, numerical precision, and alignment with principal weight subspaces. Shen et al. (2026) compare cumulative updates in on-policy distillation, rlvr , and sft , reporting low stable rank for distillation and the rlvr endpoint. These studies characterize different aspects of adaptation. Yet their rank descriptions can appear incompatible if algebraic rank, stable rank, and energy coverage are treated as interchangeable. A comparison on the same update matrix is needed to determine what each description actually implies. We address this question with an explicit spectral construction and full-spectrum measurements of selected updates.

Even a complete endpoint spectrum leaves a second question unanswered. It does not determine whether consecutive training displacements reinforce or oppose one another. Analyses of full weight matrices ( He & Cao, 2025 ) and trajectory-level linear trends ( Wang et al., 2026 ) provide complementary information, but neither an endpoint change nor a fitted trend determines the inner products between consecutive finite displacements. We therefore measure direction at specified checkpoint widths and separations. These measurements describe local alignment on the saved checkpoint grid. Differences in trajectory alignment raise a third question. How does the advantage estimator affect the direction of weight updates under a shared training schedule? We investigate this question through a controlled comparison of group-relative advantages and a learned critic with generalized advantage estimation. Holding the actor schedule and sampled prompt stream fixed connects the observed geometry to a specific change in the training procedure. These investigations provide complementary views of post-training geometry. Spectral analysis characterizes how the cumulative weight change is distributed across singular directions, while trajectory analysis examines how successive weight changes interact during training. The controlled comparison then investigates whether changing the advantage system alters these directional relationships. Together, these measurements distinguish the structure of the final update from the geometry of the path taken to reach it.

passages.text: A temporary optimization intervention can increase validation loss when it ends yet reduce it at the final training budget. We demonstrate this with temporary weight decay in Muon-trained decoder-only Transformers with 162M, 405M, 1.4B, and 3.4B parameters. For models up to 1.4B parameters, moving a fixed-duration decay window from early to late training reverses its final effect. At 162M, changing window duration alters final loss even at approximately matched total shrinkage. Most strikingly, a schedule selected at 162M and transferred without retuning to 1.4B is 0.26 nats worse than no decay when removed, overtakes it only after 73% of training, and ultimately finishes 0.028 nats better while also outperforming the best sampled constant-decay baseline. Early decay leaves a persistent weight-norm deficit, which keeps relative steps larger after the intervention ends. An approximate norm-dynamics recurrence captures the slow convergence of these relative steps, and fixed-norm replays of the measured trajectories reproduce the performance ordering and a similar loss difference. At 162M and 405M, norm-reset experiments show that smaller weight norms at the end of the decay window explain most of the final loss improvement. A separate Gram intervention exhibits related post-removal norm and relative-step dynamics. These results show that temporary optimization schedules can have delayed effects long after removal and should therefore be evaluated at the intended final training budget, not only at removal. † † date: November 12, 2026 † † correspondence: Md Rifat Arefin at rifat.arefin@mila.quebec

Temporary changes during early training are known to have lasting effects on the learned solution ( Achille et al., 2017 ; Frankle et al., 2020 ) , and prior work has shown that regularization can matter disproportionately during early learning ( Golatkar et al., 2019 ) . We study a different aspect of this phenomenon: the effect of a temporary intervention can continue to evolve after the intervention has ended, to the point that its sign or ranking changes at later checkpoints. This creates a basic problem for evaluating temporary optimization schedules. Such schedules are usually specified by an update rule and the interval over which it is applied. But when the intervention ends, the treated and reference runs generally enter the subsequent phase with different parameters and optimizer states. Their loss difference can therefore continue to evolve even though their explicit update rules are again identical. Evaluating an intervention when it is removed can consequently select a schedule that is inferior at the intended final training budget—or reject one that will eventually be beneficial.

We study this phenomenon using temporary weight decay in Muon-trained decoder-only Transformers. Weight decay provides a particularly controlled setting: turning it off cleanly separates its direct shrinkage from the training state it leaves behind. Muon also provides a useful connection between weight norms and subsequent optimization. Its matrix updates have approximately controlled magnitude, so for a given projected update norm, reducing the weight norm increases the update size relative to the current weights ( Jordan et al., 2024 ; Kosson et al., 2023 ; Wen et al., 2026 ; Liu et al., 2026 ) . Temporary decay can therefore alter subsequent optimization even after its coefficient has returned to zero. We ask two related questions: Central question. How should a temporary optimization intervention be evaluated, and what aspects of the training state carry its effect after the intervention is removed? We address the first question by varying when decay starts, how long it lasts, and when its effect is evaluated. Across models from 162M to 1.4B parameters, moving a fixed-duration decay window from early to late training reverses its final effect: early windows improve final loss, whereas a window beginning at 60 % 60\% of training hurts. At 405M, even among beneficial early schedules, the ranking changes depending on whether they are compared at a common final training budget or after the same amount of post-removal training. At 162M, changing window duration also changes final loss substantially even when total multiplicative shrinkage is approximately matched. These results separate three notions that are often conflated: when an intervention acts, how long the model trains after it is removed, and the final budget at which it is evaluated.

We address the second question by examining what remains different after decay is removed. Early decay leaves a persistent weight-norm deficit, which keeps relative steps larger than in the no-decay run long after both models resume the same update rule. An approximate recurrence accounts for the slow convergence of these relative-step trajectories. An opposite perturbation—boosting the learning rate early—raises weight norms and leaves relative steps smaller after the boost ends, as predicted by the same account. More directly, fixed-norm replays using the measured relative-step trajectories reproduce the performance ordering and a similar loss difference; swapping trajectories at the end of the decay window shows that most of the replay advantage arises from the altered steps after decay has ended. These experiments explain how an early intervention can continue to modify optimization after removal, although they do not establish that norms are the only persistent state or explain why a particular relative-step trajectory is beneficial. Together, these experiments characterize both the evaluation consequences of delayed optimization effects and one mechanism by which an early intervention can remain active through the state it leaves behind.

passages.text: Transmitting LoRA adapters to rollout workers can bottleneck distributed on-policy post-training over bandwidth-constrained networks. Lowering the training rank may limit the capacity a workload needs, while adaptive optimizer updates are difficult to compress. Rollout workers can instead reconstruct updates from gradients by maintaining replicated optimizer states. We introduce HiLo , a compressor-agnostic framework that replaces parameter transmission with compressed gradient dissemination and local optimizer replay. By applying the same decoded gradients, the learner and workers maintain consistent policy states at the same version under reproducible execution. We further develop Spar , a budget-aware gradient compressor that combines spectral truncation, adaptive rank allocation and error feedback to decouple training rank from communication cost. Experiments across on-policy distillation and reward-guided post-training show that HiLo with Spar maintains learning quality close to full synchronization while transmitting as little as 1.6% of the adapter bytes, and accelerates end-to-end updates by up to 2.2 × 2.2\times under bandwidth constraints.

We therefore ask whether synchronization must operate on parameter changes at all. For a gradient-driven optimizer with reproducible transitions, the next state is determined by the current parameters, optimizer state, gradient and update configuration. Distributed data-parallel training uses this principle to keep replicas synchronized through shared gradients and local optimizer updates ( Li et al., 2020 ) . A rollout worker can likewise reconstruct the learner’s update from the same gradient by maintaining replicated parameters and optimizer state under matched execution. This moves compression before the optimizer step, allowing established gradient-compression methods ( Lin et al., 2018 ; Vogels et al., 2019 ) to exploit gradient structure before optimizer transformations reshape the update (§ 3.3 ). passages.section: Do Pretraining Optimizer Gains Transfer to KL Distillation?
passages.text: Lavinia Ghita * Dhruv Desai * Affiliation: NVIDIA * * footnotetext: Equal contribution. Emails: lghita@nvidia.com , dhruvd@nvidia.com . Abstract. Matrix-structured optimizers can improve language-model pretraining, but it is unclear whether these gains transfer to short-horizon KL distillation from an instruction-tuned initialization. We compare AdamW and diagonal AdaGrad with two tractable Shampoo reductions, SOAP, and All-2D Muon across four dense Qwen student–teacher pairs under a common forward-KL objective and fixed training budget. Across scales, none of the evaluated matrix-structured recipes consistently improves the quality–trainer-time trade-off over the elementwise references: AdamW generally attains the lowest validation KL, while AdaGrad can be slightly faster at larger scale. SOAP often tracks AdamW in KL but incurs substantial trainer-time overhead, and the two Shampoo reductions reverse ordering across model pairs, showing that conclusions depend on the feasible recipe. These results suggest that pretraining optimizer gains do not transfer automatically to KL distillation and should be re-established for the target objective and systems regime.

We compare six distillation recipes: AdamW [ 21 ] and diagonal AdaGrad [ 2 ] as references; scalar-row-mean quarter-power and right-only half-power Shampoo; SOAP [ 6 ] ; and All-2D Muon [ 8 ] . All-2D Muon applies its spectral update to every two-dimensional parameter and Adam to one-dimensional parameters. AdamW and AdaGrad use native PyTorch implementations; the remaining methods use PyTorch/FSDP2 adaptations. SOAP matches the authors’ implementation in fixed-gradient parity tests. Trainer times are specific to these adapters. Every full-budget final configuration is evaluated with three seeds. Qwen2.5 SOAP is limited to one matched 561-step run because of its measured trainer-time overhead and is excluded from full-budget summaries. Appendices A – C document implementation details, grafting controls, selection, and final settings. Within each student–teacher pair, every method uses the forward-KL training loss in Equation 2 , with λ = 0.5 \lambda=0.5 , and global batch 144. Weight decay is zero, no learning-rate scheduler or warmup is used, and gradients are clipped to unit norm. Training uses bfloat16 FSDP2 with float32 gradient reduction. Because weight decay is zero, the PyTorch AdamW update is equivalent here to Adam; we retain the AdamW label. All methods use the same fixed budget of 1683 optimizer updates. One effective epoch is 552 updates, the number of complete batches of 144 in the 79,535 79{,}535 -example training split, so the budget runs slightly past three effective epochs. Pilot runs showed diminishing validation-KL improvements toward the end of this horizon.

The three Qwen3 pairs use 72 NVIDIA GB200 accelerators across 18 four-accelerator nodes. The larger Qwen2.5 32 ​ B ← 72 ​ B 32\mathrm{B}\leftarrow 72\mathrm{B} pair uses 144 accelerators across 36 such nodes to accommodate the dense teacher and student. We use trainer time for elapsed time spent in training, validation, and improvement-triggered checkpointing; it excludes model loading, queueing, and final model export. We evaluate quality using two criteria. The within-budget criterion is the three-seed mean of each run’s minimum validation KL observed during 1683 steps, corresponding to validation-based checkpoint selection. The matched-step criterion compares the three-seed mean trajectories at common evaluation steps. Absolute KL is compared only within a student–teacher pair. We report means with one standard deviation and interpret both quality views together with trainer time rather than combine them into a single score. Comparisons are descriptive and use neither hypothesis tests nor a fixed threshold for small KL differences. We describe an advantage as consistent only when the same qualitative ordering recurs across model pairs.

passages.text: Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) often underperforms full fine-tuning, especially in heterogeneous and continual-learning settings in which substantial forgetting occurs. In general, it suffers from an undesirable learning–forgetting trade-off across diverse fine-tuning settings. We identify a potential contributor: LoRA adapters, especially high-rank ones, frequently fail to realize the available capacity afforded by the configured rank. Specifically, we find that standard LoRA updates have effective rank far below their configured rank, limiting how broadly the update energy is distributed. Therefore, we propose training mechanisms that optimize the original objective while maximizing adapter effective rank. Our main method adds a simple, stable, differentiable, and SVD-free Rényi-2 effective-rank regularizer to the language-modeling loss. We also connect capacity maximization to norm-bounded updates. In mixed-domain rank sweeps on three models evaluated with multiple random seeds, a penalty weight of λ = 0.01 \lambda=0.01 lowers mean Wiki perplexity at every tested rank of at least 16 16 relative to unpenalized LoRA. Mean training perplexity improves or increases by at most 0.02 0.02 in all but one model–rank comparison. Single-task and scheduling experiments further show that the balance between learning and retention depends on the configuration. We also observe that several LoRA variants in the literature also suffer from the identified capacity issue, and our approach provides a complementary axis of improvement to LoRA-based parameter-efficient fine-tuning. These results suggest that effective rank is not only a post-hoc diagnostic of adapter quality, but a trainable objective for improving the learning–forgetting frontier. Our code is available at

We propose SCALAR , which achieves performance comparable to LoRA with substantially fewer trainable parameters, lower peak training memory, and higher throughput. SCALAR constructs a fixed input basis from task activations and assigns a random output dictionary to each input direction. Fine-tuning learns only layer-specific scalar coefficients, reducing gradient and optimizer-state storage. Grouped computation aggregates output atoms before applying the adapter to token activations, while dictionary sharing across compatible layers reduces fixed-basis storage. Experiments on commonsense reasoning, mathematical reasoning, code generation, and knowledge evaluation after instruction tuning demonstrate effective adaptation at small trainable budgets. On commonsense reasoning, SCALAR achieves accuracy comparable to LoRA with about 4% of its trainable parameters. System measurements on Qwen2.5-7B show 20% lower peak training memory and 6% higher throughput than LoRA. The combination of adaptation quality, a compact trainable state, and training efficiency makes SCALAR a promising approach to resource-constrained fine-tuning. 1 1 footnotetext: Work done during an internship at OPPO AI-Center. 1 1 footnotetext: National University of Defense Technology. How can we construct a task-relevant fixed update space that maintains adaptation quality with few trainable coefficients, low memory use, and high throughput? We first investigate this question through a learned-direction reweighting diagnostic. We train a rank-one LoRA adapter, freeze its learned update direction for each adapted matrix, and re-optimize one scalar coefficient per matrix. On a 7B model, the reweighting stage optimizes 196 196 parameters compared with LoRA’s 2,523,136 2{,}523{,}136 , and achieves similar optimization behavior and downstream accuracy. This observation motivates constructing informative directions before fine-tuning and adapting through a small set of coefficients. We propose SCALAR : Subspace-Calibrated Adaptation via Layerwise Atom Reweighting . SCALAR constructs a fixed input basis from the leading singular vectors of downstream activations and assigns a separate random output dictionary to each input direction. Learning the coefficients selects an effective output vector within each of these fixed output subspaces. With R R input directions and H H output atoms per direction, each adapted matrix has K = R ​ H K=RH trainable coefficients and an update rank of at most R R . The output atoms in each group are aggregated before application to the activations, so the token-dependent matrix multiplications operate on R R effective directions. Compatible layers can also share the frozen output dictionaries.

Experiments on commonsense reasoning, mathematical reasoning, and code generation show competitive performance with compact trainable budgets. On Qwen2.5-7B and LLaMA3-8B, SCALAR approaches rank-8 LoRA accuracy on commonsense reasoning using about 4% of its trainable parameters. System measurements demonstrate lower peak training memory and higher throughput, giving the compact parameterization practical value during training. Our analysis builds on activation coverage to examine the initial gradient signal and connects it to the coefficients trained by SCALAR . Compatible layers share their fixed output dictionaries to reduce basis storage. Analysis and diagnostic evidence. Building on activation-subspace analysis, we characterize the effect of gradient-weighted activation geometry on the initial learning signal and derive its connection to SCALAR ’s coefficients. A learned-direction reweighting diagnostic motivates adaptation within informative fixed update spaces.

Language-model post-training changes a model’s behavior by changing its weights. Supervised fine-tuning ( sft ) learns from demonstration responses, while reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards ( rlvr ) learns from sampled responses scored by an automatic checker. Weight-space measurements describe how these procedures alter a pretrained model and inform methods that operate on weight differences, including task arithmetic and low-rank adaptation ( Ilharco et al., 2023 ; Hu et al., 2022 ) . Interpreting those measurements requires separating the mathematical object being measured from the functional applied to it. That distinction matters when comparing recent accounts of post-training geometry. Mukherjee et al. (2025) report sparse, nearly full-algebraic-rank rlvr updates. Zhu et al. (2025) analyze update localization, numerical precision, and alignment with principal weight subspaces. Shen et al. (2026) compare cumulative updates in on-policy distillation, rlvr , and sft , reporting low stable rank for distillation and the rlvr endpoint. These studies characterize different aspects of adaptation. Yet their rank descriptions can appear incompatible if algebraic rank, stable rank, and energy coverage are treated as interchangeable. A comparison on the same update matrix is needed to determine what each description actually implies. We address this question with an explicit spectral construction and full-spectrum measurements of selected updates.

Even a complete endpoint spectrum leaves a second question unanswered. It does not determine whether consecutive training displacements reinforce or oppose one another. Analyses of full weight matrices ( He & Cao, 2025 ) and trajectory-level linear trends ( Wang et al., 2026 ) provide complementary information, but neither an endpoint change nor a fitted trend determines the inner products between consecutive finite displacements. We therefore measure direction at specified checkpoint widths and separations. These measurements describe local alignment on the saved checkpoint grid. Differences in trajectory alignment raise a third question. How does the advantage estimator affect the direction of weight updates under a shared training schedule? We investigate this question through a controlled comparison of group-relative advantages and a learned critic with generalized advantage estimation. Holding the actor schedule and sampled prompt stream fixed connects the observed geometry to a specific change in the training procedure. These investigations provide complementary views of post-training geometry. Spectral analysis characterizes how the cumulative weight change is distributed across singular directions, while trajectory analysis examines how successive weight changes interact during training. The controlled comparison then investigates whether changing the advantage system alters these directional relationships. Together, these measurements distinguish the structure of the final update from the geometry of the path taken to reach it.

We demonstrate this with temporary weight decay in Muon-trained decoder-only Transformers with 162M, 405M, 1.4B, and 3.4B parameters. For models up to 1.4B parameters, moving a fixed-duration decay window from early to late training reverses its final effect. At 162M, changing window duration alters final loss even at approximately matched total shrinkage. Most strikingly, a schedule selected at 162M and transferred without retuning to 1.4B is 0.26 nats worse than no decay when removed, overtakes it only after 73% of training, and ultimately finishes 0.028 nats better while also outperforming the best sampled constant-decay baseline. Early decay leaves a persistent weight-norm deficit, which keeps relative steps larger after the intervention ends. An approximate norm-dynamics recurrence captures the slow convergence of these relative steps, and fixed-norm replays of the measured trajectories reproduce the performance ordering and a similar loss difference. At 162M and 405M, norm-reset experiments show that smaller weight norms at the end of the decay window explain most of the final loss improvement. A separate Gram intervention exhibits related post-removal norm and relative-step dynamics. These results show that temporary optimization schedules can have delayed effects long after removal and should therefore be evaluated at the intended final training budget, not only at removal. † † date: November 12, 2026 † † correspondence: Md Rifat Arefin at rifat.arefin@mila.quebec

Temporary changes during early training are known to have lasting effects on the learned solution ( Achille et al., 2017 ; Frankle et al., 2020 ) , and prior work has shown that regularization can matter disproportionately during early learning ( Golatkar et al., 2019 ) . We study a different aspect of this phenomenon: the effect of a temporary intervention can continue to evolve after the intervention has ended, to the point that its sign or ranking changes at later checkpoints. This creates a basic problem for evaluating temporary optimization schedules. Such schedules are usually specified by an update rule and the interval over which it is applied. But when the intervention ends, the treated and reference runs generally enter the subsequent phase with different parameters and optimizer states. Their loss difference can therefore continue to evolve even though their explicit update rules are again identical. Evaluating an intervention when it is removed can consequently select a schedule that is inferior at the intended final training budget—or reject one that will eventually be beneficial.

We study this phenomenon using temporary weight decay in Muon-trained decoder-only Transformers. Weight decay provides a particularly controlled setting: turning it off cleanly separates its direct shrinkage from the training state it leaves behind. Muon also provides a useful connection between weight norms and subsequent optimization. Its matrix updates have approximately controlled magnitude, so for a given projected update norm, reducing the weight norm increases the update size relative to the current weights ( Jordan et al., 2024 ; Kosson et al., 2023 ; Wen et al., 2026 ; Liu et al., 2026 ) . Temporary decay can therefore alter subsequent optimization even after its coefficient has returned to zero. We ask two related questions: Central question. How should a temporary optimization intervention be evaluated, and what aspects of the training state carry its effect after the intervention is removed? We address the first question by varying when decay starts, how long it lasts, and when its effect is evaluated. Across models from 162M to 1.4B parameters, moving a fixed-duration decay window from early to late training reverses its final effect: early windows improve final loss, whereas a window beginning at 60 % 60\% of training hurts. At 405M, even among beneficial early schedules, the ranking changes depending on whether they are compared at a common final training budget or after the same amount of post-removal training. At 162M, changing window duration also changes final loss substantially even when total multiplicative shrinkage is approximately matched. These results separate three notions that are often conflated: when an intervention acts, how long the model trains after it is removed, and the final budget at which it is evaluated.

We address the second question by examining what remains different after decay is removed. Early decay leaves a persistent weight-norm deficit, which keeps relative steps larger than in the no-decay run long after both models resume the same update rule. An approximate recurrence accounts for the slow convergence of these relative-step trajectories. An opposite perturbation—boosting the learning rate early—raises weight norms and leaves relative steps smaller after the boost ends, as predicted by the same account. More directly, fixed-norm replays using the measured relative-step trajectories reproduce the performance ordering and a similar loss difference; swapping trajectories at the end of the decay window shows that most of the replay advantage arises from the altered steps after decay has ended. These experiments explain how an early intervention can continue to modify optimization after removal, although they do not establish that norms are the only persistent state or explain why a particular relative-step trajectory is beneficial. Together, these experiments characterize both the evaluation consequences of delayed optimization effects and one mechanism by which an early intervention can remain active through the state it leaves behind.

passages.section: Do Pretraining Optimizer Gains Transfer to KL Distillation?
passages.text: Lavinia Ghita * Dhruv Desai * Affiliation: NVIDIA * * footnotetext: Equal contribution. Emails: lghita@nvidia.com , dhruvd@nvidia.com . Abstract. Matrix-structured optimizers can improve language-model pretraining, but it is unclear whether these gains transfer to short-horizon KL distillation from an instruction-tuned initialization. We compare AdamW and diagonal AdaGrad with two tractable Shampoo reductions, SOAP, and All-2D Muon across four dense Qwen student–teacher pairs under a common forward-KL objective and fixed training budget. Across scales, none of the evaluated matrix-structured recipes consistently improves the quality–trainer-time trade-off over the elementwise references: AdamW generally attains the lowest validation KL, while AdaGrad can be slightly faster at larger scale. SOAP often tracks AdamW in KL but incurs substantial trainer-time overhead, and the two Shampoo reductions reverse ordering across model pairs, showing that conclusions depend on the feasible recipe. These results suggest that pretraining optimizer gains do not transfer automatically to KL distillation and should be re-established for the target objective and systems regime.

We compare six distillation recipes: AdamW [ 21 ] and diagonal AdaGrad [ 2 ] as references; scalar-row-mean quarter-power and right-only half-power Shampoo; SOAP [ 6 ] ; and All-2D Muon [ 8 ] . All-2D Muon applies its spectral update to every two-dimensional parameter and Adam to one-dimensional parameters. AdamW and AdaGrad use native PyTorch implementations; the remaining methods use PyTorch/FSDP2 adaptations. SOAP matches the authors’ implementation in fixed-gradient parity tests. Trainer times are specific to these adapters. Every full-budget final configuration is evaluated with three seeds. Qwen2.5 SOAP is limited to one matched 561-step run because of its measured trainer-time overhead and is excluded from full-budget summaries. Appendices A – C document implementation details, grafting controls, selection, and final settings. Within each student–teacher pair, every method uses the forward-KL training loss in Equation 2 , with λ = 0.5 \lambda=0.5 , and global batch 144. Weight decay is zero, no learning-rate scheduler or warmup is used, and gradients are clipped to unit norm. Training uses bfloat16 FSDP2 with float32 gradient reduction. Because weight decay is zero, the PyTorch AdamW update is equivalent here to Adam; we retain the AdamW label. All methods use the same fixed budget of 1683 optimizer updates. One effective epoch is 552 updates, the number of complete batches of 144 in the 79,535 79{,}535 -example training split, so the budget runs slightly past three effective epochs. Pilot runs showed diminishing validation-KL improvements toward the end of this horizon.

The three Qwen3 pairs use 72 NVIDIA GB200 accelerators across 18 four-accelerator nodes. The larger Qwen2.5 32 ​ B ← 72 ​ B 32\mathrm{B}\leftarrow 72\mathrm{B} pair uses 144 accelerators across 36 such nodes to accommodate the dense teacher and student. We use trainer time for elapsed time spent in training, validation, and improvement-triggered checkpointing; it excludes model loading, queueing, and final model export. We evaluate quality using two criteria. The within-budget criterion is the three-seed mean of each run’s minimum validation KL observed during 1683 steps, corresponding to validation-based checkpoint selection. The matched-step criterion compares the three-seed mean trajectories at common evaluation steps. Absolute KL is compared only within a student–teacher pair. We report means with one standard deviation and interpret both quality views together with trainer time rather than combine them into a single score. Comparisons are descriptive and use neither hypothesis tests nor a fixed threshold for small KL differences. We describe an advantage as consistent only when the same qualitative ordering recurs across model pairs.

passages.text: Within the fixed budget, the evaluated matrix-structured methods show no validation-KL advantage over AdamW that persists across model pairs (Figure 1 ). Figure 1: Minimum validation KL within 1683 1683 steps: three-seed means of per-seed minima, with one-standard-deviation error bars. Lower is better. Qwen3 pairs use 72 GPUs and Qwen2.5 uses 144; Qwen2.5 SOAP was not extended beyond one matched 561-step run. AdamW, SOAP, and All-2D Muon are closely grouped at 0.6 ​ B 0.6\mathrm{B} ; AdamW is lower than SOAP and All-2D Muon at 4 ​ B 4\mathrm{B} and 14 ​ B 14\mathrm{B} , and lower than AdaGrad on all four pairs. The Shampoo comparison is pair-dependent. Each Shampoo point is a pair-specific, validation-selected configuration (Appendix C ), not a family-wide optimum under an equal tuning budget. Right-only half-power Shampoo has lower validation KL at 0.6 ​ B 0.6\mathrm{B} , whereas scalar-row-mean quarter-power is lower at 4 ​ B 4\mathrm{B} ; their nearly identical trainer-time ratios indicate recipe dependence rather than a quality–trainer-time trade-off. Scalar-row-mean quarter-power remains above AdamW at 14 ​ B 14\mathrm{B} and Qwen2.5 32 ​ B 32\mathrm{B} . The selected k = 10 k=10 right-only half-power configuration is likewise above AdamW at 14 ​ B 14\mathrm{B} , and the Qwen2.5 32 ​ B 32\mathrm{B} configuration is above both AdamW and scalar-row-mean quarter-power. Given that the teacher, student architecture, matrix geometry, and factor coverage change together, these cross-pair differences do not establish a scale trend.

Trainer-time results sharpen the quality comparison: every matrix-structured method with completed results adds trainer time relative to AdamW, whereas AdaGrad becomes slightly faster than AdamW at the larger evaluated student sizes (Figure 3 ). This is consistent with AdaGrad’s lighter elementwise update: it maintains one accumulator rather than AdamW’s first- and second-moment states, reducing optimizer-state traffic and pointwise work. The Qwen2.5 experiments use 144 GPUs, however, and therefore do not provide a pure scale continuation of the fixed 72-GPU regime used for Qwen3. Figure 3: Trainer time normalized per pair and seed to AdamW ( 1.0 1.0 ); bars show three-seed means with one-standard-deviation error bars. Qwen3 pairs use 72 GPUs and Qwen2.5 uses 144; ratios are within-pair. The matched 561-step Qwen2.5 SOAP run took 4.31 × 4.31\times AdamW trainer time and was not extended. Among the evaluated matrix-structured methods, the two Shampoo reductions have the smallest overhead and nearly identical trainer time on their shared completed pairs. Their reversal in validation KL therefore reflects the optimizer recipe rather than different compute budgets. All-2D Muon becomes more expensive on the larger pairs. SOAP is qualitatively different: it requires roughly two to three times AdamW’s trainer time on the Qwen3 pairs. Online teacher inference, validation, and checkpointing reduce the optimizer’s share of total time. These ratios therefore measure systems-level protocol overhead, not student-only optimizer-kernel overhead, and may understate the latter.

At Qwen2.5 32 ​ B ← 72 ​ B 32\mathrm{B}\leftarrow 72\mathrm{B} , SOAP incurred substantially greater trainer time than AdamW without a clear improvement in validation KL at the matched 561-step horizon. Its unblocked FSDP2 adapter gathers full gradients and moments, replicates matrix factors, and refreshes bases frequently (Appendix A ). Model sharding does not distribute this optimizer work, so we did not extend SOAP.
